ptarmigan.e: From Scottish Gaelic tarmachan, of unknown origin. The pt- comes from a mistaken belief in a Greek origin, as if related to ptero- (“wing”).

s.d: large Arctic and subarctic grouse with feathered feet and usually white winter plumage
Any of three species of small grouse in the genus Lagopus found in subarctic tundra areas of North America and Eurasia.
of or relating to the study of ferns
Relating to pteridology.

A person who studies ferns and other pteridophytes.

s.d: the branch of botany that studies ferns
(uncountable) The scientific study of ferns and other pteridophytes.
plants having vascular tissue and reproducing by spores

Any plant of the division Pteridophyta, of simple vascular plants that reproduce via spores rather than seeds and that alternate generations of diploid (sporophyte) and haploid (gametophyte or prothallus) forms, the diploid generally being larger and more conspicuous.
x: Ferns, lycopods, and scouring rushes are all pteridophytes.
Most pteridophytes are homosporous, producing one type of spore that germinates to produce a potentially bisexual gametophyte.

s.d: an extinct seed-producing fernlike plant of the order Cycadofilicales (or group Pteridospermae)
Any of various extinct gymnosperms, of the division Pteridospermatophyta, resembling ferns, but producing seeds instead of spores

pterion.e: From French ptérion, from ptère (“wing of the sphenoid bone”) + -ion, from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

s.d: the craniometric point in the region of the sphenoid fontanelle
The point corresponding with the posterior end of the sphenoparietal suture; known as the weakest part of the skull.
x: Then standing before a closet mirror, he put the automatic to his head, at the point of the pterion, and pressed the comfortably concaved trigger.

pterodactyl.e: From French ptérodactyle, a term coined by Cuvier from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”). By surface analysis, ptero- + -dactyl.

s.d: extinct flying reptile
A pterosaur of the genus Pterodactylus.
Any pterosaur.
x: He described also the iguanodon and the pterodactyl - two of the first of the wonders which they had encountered.
Had a pterodactyl swooped down from those old-time crags, it would hardly have been out of place.

s.d: southern Australian plant having feathery hairs surrounding the fruit

pterosaur.e: From ptero- + -saur, literally “wing lizard”, from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “feather, wing”) and σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard, reptile”).

s.d: an extinct reptile of the Jurassic and Cretaceous having a bird-like beak and membranous wings supported by the very long fourth digit of each forelimb
Any flying reptile, of the extinct order †Pterosauria, including the pterodactyls.
x: Batsquatch, pterosaurs and the River Man. She had three weeks in Washington State tracking down the local legends. There was nothing ordinary about her job as the biologist on the television show Cryptid or Hoax?

s.d: a B vitamin that is essential for cell growth and reproduction
(dated, uncountable) folic acid, a polycyclic heterocyclic carboxylic acid of the vitamin B complex, essential for cell growth and reproduction.
a B vitamin that is essential for cell growth and reproduction
(uncountable) folic acid

pterygium.e: From Ancient Greek πτερύγιον (pterúgion), diminutive of πτέρυξ (ptérux, “wing”). By surface analysis, pteryg- + -ium.

s.d: either of two thickened triangular layers of conjunctiva extending from the nasal edge of the eye to the cornea; it arises from irritation of the pinguecula
An abnormal mass of tissue in the corner of the eye that obstructs vision.
A generalized limb of a vertebrate.
muscle descending from the sphenoid bone to the lower jaw
Either of two muscles arising respectively from the lateral and medial surfaces of the lateral pterygoid process which serve to move the mandible forwards and to the side.
a plexus of veins draining the region of the pterygoid muscles and draining into the internal maxillary and anterior facial veins
two bony processes descending from the body of the sphenoid bone
Each of a pair of projections extending downward from each side of the sphenoid bone in humans and other mammals.
any of various amines (such as putrescine or cadaverine) formed by the action of putrefactive bacteria

ptomaine.e: From French ptomaïne, from Italian ptomaina, from Ancient Greek πτῶμα (ptôma, “corpse”).

s.d: any of various amines (such as putrescine or cadaverine) formed by the action of putrefactive bacteria
a term for food poisoning that is no longer in scientific use; food poisoning was once thought to be caused by ingesting ptomaines
(dated, uncountable) Food poisoning.
x: Elinor said: "One used to be rather afraid of eating fish pastes. There have been cases of ptomaine poisoning from them, haven't there?"
You remember Leonard Skinner. He got ptomaine poisoning last night after dinner.

s.d: a term for food poisoning that is no longer in scientific use; food poisoning was once thought to be caused by ingesting ptomaines

ptosis.e: From Ancient Greek πτῶσις (ptôsis, “falling, fall”), from πίπτω (píptō, “to fall down”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix). First used in 1710.

s.d: drooping of the upper eyelid caused by muscle paralysis and weakness
(uncountable) The prolapse of a bodily organ, especially drooping of the eyelid or the breasts.
an amylase secreted in saliva
(uncountable) A form of amylase found in saliva that breaks down starch into maltose and dextrin.
excessive flow of saliva
(uncountable) sialorrhea
calculus in a salivary gland
expel or eject (saliva or phlegm or sputum) from the mouth
x: The father of the victim spat at the alleged murderer

s.d: (rare) To spit.
(rare) To salivate.
